What Happens When an NFL Bet Pushes — And How It Changes Parlays and Teasers

Published October 11, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Our guide to NFL half-point hooks covers why books hang a .5 off most spreads so a push almost never happens on the main line. But "almost never" isn't "never" — totals still land on whole numbers constantly, pick'em moneylines exist, and plenty of secondary markets get posted without a hook at all. When one of those does land dead on the number, what happens to your money depends entirely on what kind of ticket that bet was sitting on. A single straight bet pushing is the simplest case in sports betting. The same push buried inside a six-leg parlay or a two-team teaser triggers a completely different set of rules, and misunderstanding those rules is a common way bettors misjudge what a ticket is actually worth before the last leg settles.

  2. What a push does inside a parlay
  3. A worked example: a five-leg parlay with one push

How a push settles on a straight bet

Start with the simplest version, because it's the one most bettors already understand correctly. If you bet $110 on a team at -3 and the final margin is exactly 3 points, the bet pushes: your $110 is returned in full, with no winnings and no loss of vig. The sportsbook doesn't keep a cent and you don't gain a cent. Functionally, it's as if the bet never happened — your account balance is identical to what it would have been had you never placed the wager. That's true whether it's a spread, a total, or a rare pick'em moneyline that technically allows a tie in regulation before overtime intervenes.

This is also why a push is sometimes called a "no action" bet on a settlement sheet, and why some operators use the two terms almost interchangeably in their grading systems. The distinction matters more once you leave the world of single bets, because "no action" is precisely the phrase that describes what a pushed leg does to everything stacked around it.

What a push does inside a parlay

A parlay only pays out if every single leg wins. That's the entire premise of the bet, and it raises an obvious question: if one leg is graded a push instead of a win or a loss, does the whole parlay just die along with it? The answer, at essentially every regulated U.S. sportsbook, is no. Standard parlay rules treat a pushed leg as removed from the bet entirely, and the parlay simply recalculates using whatever legs remain.

A four-leg parlay with one push becomes a three-leg parlay. A two-leg parlay with one push becomes a single straight bet, paid at that leg's own odds. Your other legs still need to win on their own merits — a push doesn't bail out a losing parlay, and it doesn't inflate the importance of the legs that are left. It just quietly exits the ticket and takes its piece of the combined odds with it.

The part that surprises people: a pushed leg lowers your potential payout, not because the book is punishing you, but because the parlay's odds were built by multiplying every leg's price together. Remove one leg's price from that multiplication and the total payout shrinks to match whatever's left — even though you didn't technically lose anything.

A worked example: a five-leg parlay with one push

Say you build a five-leg NFL parlay, each leg priced at standard -110 (roughly 1.91 in decimal odds), on a $25 stake. Multiply five legs of -110 together and the combined payout sits a little north of 24-to-1, turning $25 into roughly $630 in total returns if every leg hits. Now suppose one of those five legs — a total that landed exactly on the number — pushes. The book removes that leg's -110 price from the calculation entirely, leaving a four-leg parlay built from the remaining prices.

ScenarioLegs countedApprox. payout on $25 (all -110 legs)
All 5 legs win, none push5~$630 total return
4 legs win, 1 leg pushes4~$328 total return
3 legs win, 1 push, 1 lossn/a — parlay loses$0 (one actual loss still kills the ticket)

Notice what the push did and didn't do. It didn't cost you the parlay — the other four legs still needed to win on their own, and they did in this example. But it did shrink the payout from roughly $630 to roughly $328, because the parlay is now being priced off four legs instead of five. A push is neutral for your win/loss record and your stake, but it is not neutral for your payout size the moment more than one leg is involved.

Pushes inside a teaser work differently

Teasers move the spread or total on every leg in your favor by an agreed number of points, which is exactly why our teasers vs. parlays guide and the teasers crossing 3 and 7 guide both exist — teasers are priced and used differently enough from straight parlays to deserve their own treatment, and pushes are one more place that difference shows up. Because a teaser deliberately buys extra points specifically to land on softer, more push-prone numbers, teaser legs push more often in practice than ordinary spread bets do.

The settlement rule for a push inside a teaser mirrors the parlay rule in spirit — a pushed leg is removed rather than treated as a loss — but with one twist: at most books, if a teaser pushes down to a single remaining leg, that leg is paid out at reduced teaser-specific odds rather than at the leg's normal straight-bet price, and some books instead grade a teaser that pushes down to one leg as a straight win at even money or close to it. The exact handling varies by operator and is spelled out in the house rules on teaser payout grids, so it's worth checking a specific book's rules before assuming either outcome. What's consistent everywhere is the core principle: a push removes that leg and reprices the rest, exactly as it does in a standard parlay.

Same-game parlays and correlated pushes

Same-game parlays add a wrinkle worth flagging separately, since our same-game parlay guide covers how correlation between legs from the same game already complicates the payout math. A push inside an SGP settles using the same remove-and-reprice logic as any other parlay, but because SGP legs are drawn from a single game, a push on one leg (say, a total) can sit right next to a leg that's directly affected by the same final score (say, a spread). Each leg is still graded independently on its own terms — the total pushing doesn't change whether the spread leg separately won or lost — but it's a useful reminder that in an SGP, "independent" grading doesn't mean the outcomes themselves were independent events.

Where NFL pushes actually show up

Given how aggressively books hook the spread at 3 and 7, most NFL pushes in practice come from totals, not spreads. Totals are far more likely to be posted on a clean whole number — 44, 41, 47 — because the push-avoidance logic that drives spread hooking doesn't apply as cleanly to totals, where the "key number" distribution of combined final scores is flatter and less concentrated than the margin-of-victory distribution that makes 3 and 7 special on the spread side. Alternate lines and player-prop markets can also land on push-friendly whole numbers more often than the heavily-hooked main spread does, since books don't apply the same half-point convention as consistently across every secondary market. If you're stacking totals and alternate lines into a parlay, you're statistically more likely to see a push turn up somewhere on the ticket than if you'd stuck to standard spreads.

What this means for how you build a ticket

None of this should change whether you like a bet — a push is a wash either way, not a loss to fear. What it should change is how you estimate a parlay's actual payout odds before you place it. If you're leaning on round-number totals or alternate lines to fill out a big parlay, build in the expectation that one of those legs has a real, non-trivial chance of pushing rather than winning outright, and that your realistic payout sits somewhere between the full posted number and the reduced figure you'd get with one leg stripped out. For straight bets, a push is simply the market telling you the game landed exactly where the number said it should — no better, no worse.

Frequently asked questions

Do I get my money back right away if a bet pushes?

Yes — once the result is officially graded, your stake is credited back to your account balance in full, typically on the same settlement timeline the book uses for wins and losses on that market.

Can an entire parlay push if every leg pushes?

In the rare case where every leg in a parlay pushes, the entire parlay is treated as no action and your full stake is returned, since there's nothing left to price a payout off of.

Does a push count as a loss for promotional wagering requirements or odds-boost eligibility?

Generally no — because a push returns your stake and settles as no action, it typically doesn't count toward wagering requirements or promotional qualifying bets the way a win or loss would, though the exact treatment is set by each operator's own promo terms.

Why do some two-leg parlays become a single bet instead of just voiding entirely when one leg pushes?

Because the push only removes the pushed leg from the bet, not the entire ticket. With one leg remaining, there's still a valid, gradable bet left, so the book settles it as a straight wager at that leg's own price rather than canceling the whole thing.

Are push rules the same for parlays at every sportsbook?

The core "remove the leg and reprice" principle is close to universal, but the exact wording — especially for teasers that push down to one leg — is set by each book's own house rules, so it's worth checking the specific terms on markets you bet often.
